notes:
I couldn't cover the whole brief. I found good material from the older commentaries, Guzik and Pett, but nothing for parts 2 and 3:

- **Differences between Protestant traditions:** I found no place where the traditions actually disagree about these verses. The commentators largely agree; where they differ, it's on technical details.
- **Other views:** I found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites, netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org, or prosperity / word of faith teaching on this passage.

The only notes from a named tradition are Wesley and Benson (Methodist) on v. 51 and Barnes (Presbyterian) in several places. I ran out of searches before I could reach the sites for parts 2 and 3. Verses 28, 29, 31–37, 40–45 and 50 are thinly covered.

**v. 27**
- Pulpit Commentary: the description of the stands and basins (vv. 27–39) is extremely obscure. What is clear is that the stands were simply bases for the basins, box-shaped, about six feet square and four and a half feet high. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-27.htm
- Gill: the stand was square so the basin would sit firmly on it, and three cubits high so the priests could reach in and wash the sacrifices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-27.htm
- Ellicott: the whole unit stood tall, probably to bring it almost level with the bronze altar, which was 15 feet high. Each basin may have been a smaller copy of the Sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-27.htm
- Text difference: the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) gives each stand as five cubits long and six cubits high. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-7-commentary

**vv. 27–29 (design)**
- Ellicott: some details are unclear, and the King James translators clearly got parts of them wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-27.html
- Benson: the King James phrase "a base above" is very unclear, but probably means the top of the stand, which acted as a base for the basin. The "additions" were either footings for the carved lions and oxen or just more decoration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-27.htm
- Pett: a laver stand found at Larnaka (Cyprus) was decorated with sphinxes (the pagan counterpart of cherubim) and stylised palm trees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-7.html

**v. 30**
- Pulpit: the basins were used to wash parts of the burnt offerings (2 Chronicles 4:6). They had to be emptied and refilled constantly, so they needed wheels to go back and forth between the Sea and the altar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-30.htm
- Poole disagrees. He thinks the wheels sat on bronze plates and only held the stand up, because the stands were fixed in place (v. 39). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-30.htm
- Barnes: "plates" should read "bronze axles." The "undersetters" (literally "shoulders") were probably brackets running from the corners up to the rim of the basin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-30.htm

**vv. 32–33**
- Ellicott: the wheels were only about 27 inches high, with hubs, rims and spokes all cast in bronze. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-27.htm

**vv. 35–37**
- Ellicott: each stand had a raised round support about nine inches high with a circular opening. The basin rested over it, and brackets at the corners held it in place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-27.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the stands were elegant and well suited to their job, and all exactly the same in shape and size. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm

**v. 38**
- What "four cubits" means is debated:
  - Benson thinks it is the basin's width across, not its height. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm
  - Pulpit says it could be either. Keil chooses width, but if it were height the whole unit would be about 13 feet tall; Pulpit explains that by the height of the altar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm
  - Barnes, assuming height, concludes the water must have been drawn off through taps. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-kings-7.html
- Keil: the basins must have been shaped like wide, open shells. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm
- Purpose: Clarke says the basins were for washing the burnt-offering animals, while the Sea was for the priests to wash in. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-38.html Pulpit adds that ten basins were not too many, given how many animals were sometimes offered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm
- Spiritual readings:
  - Gill sees the basins as a picture of the full cleansing Christ's blood provides. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm
  - Trapp says they show how filthy sin is and why Christ's blood is needed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-kings-7.html
  - Matthew Henry: priests and sacrifices must be washed in the laver of Christ's blood, and we must wash often. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm
- Pett suggests ten may stand for one basin per commandment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-7.html
- Ahaz later removed the basins, though not the stands (2 Kings 16:17). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-7-commentary

**v. 39**
- Benson: "right side" means the south side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-38.htm
- Matthew Henry: the stands could be moved when needed but normally stood in two rows of five. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_007.cfm

**v. 40**
- Pett: this verse and vv. 13–14 frame Hiram's work as a unit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-7.html
- Pett also compares Hiram with Bezalel, who made the tabernacle furnishings. Hiram is described with similar words, but unlike Bezalel he is not said to be filled with God's Spirit, and he was only half Israelite. Pett reads this as hinting that Solomon's temple was more man-driven than the tabernacle. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-7.html

**vv. 41–45**
- Guzik: Huram made the furnishings broadly on the pattern of the tabernacle's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/
- Grant: Chronicles credits Solomon with all the building, while vv. 40–45 credit the bronze work to Hiram. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-kings-7.html

**v. 46**
- Location: Succoth was east of the Jordan near the Jabbok ford, and Zarethan was on the river bank in western Manasseh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-46.htm
- Why cast here? Some said it kept the smoke away from Jerusalem, but the commentator quoted (from a note in Bagster's Bible) says the real reason was the soil, which is rich in marl (clay). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-46.htm
- Coffman: excavations at Succoth (Tell Deir Alla) show it was a metalworking centre. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-46.html
- Gill: Hiram did the work; it is credited to the king because he ordered it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-46.htm

**v. 47**
- Pett: there was so much bronze that weighing it was pointless, so no figure went into the royal records. This shows how valuable the work was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-7.html

**v. 48**
- The golden altar is the incense altar (Ellicott, JFB). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-48.htm Keil says it was cedar overlaid with gold, like the tabernacle's altar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-48.htm
- One table or ten? 2 Chronicles 4:8 mentions ten tables. Guzik says Kings describes them together as one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/ Keil says bread was normally laid on only one table. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-48.htm
- Gill: everything was made new except the ark, mercy seat and cherubim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-48.htm
- Matthew Henry: Christ is now the Temple, the Altar, the Sacrifice and the Bread of Life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-48.htm
- Text difference: the Septuagint says Solomon "took the furniture which Chiram made." https://biblehub.com/1_kings/7-48.htm

**v. 49**
- Henry: there was still only one incense altar, as Christ's intercession is one, but ten tables and ten lampstands. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_007.cfm
- Coffman objects: God's pattern (Exodus 25) gave the lampstand three branches on each side, so where did five on each side come from? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-48.html
- Pett: if Solomon had seen the lampstands as picturing God as the nation's light, he would surely have made only one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-7.html
- Constable: gold inside the temple and bronze outside. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-49.html Smith's commentary reads bronze as a symbol of judgment and gold as a symbol of heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-48.html

**v. 50**
- Keil: the gold "hinges" were either hinges or, more likely, the sockets the door pegs turned in. No new item was made for the Most Holy Place, because Moses' ark was placed there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-51.htm

**v. 51**
- Did Solomon use David's gold? Clarke thinks this verse suggests he did not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-51.html Gill thinks only the leftover was stored, and Solomon did use David's bronze. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-51.htm Pulpit says there was clearly a large surplus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-51.htm
- Wesley (Methodist) agrees it was the leftover. Benson (Methodist) says it was kept for repairs and running the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-51.html
- Barnes (Presbyterian): it included war spoils and gifts from Toi of Hamath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-51.htm
- Ellicott: David gave in the spirit of 1 Chronicles 29:14, giving God what was already his. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-51.htm
- Henry: children should not take back what their parents dedicated to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-7.html
- Pett: the closing words end the third section of the passage. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-7.html
